title: Core dental service to be considered in Northern Ireland
html:
The Department of Health for Northern Ireland is developing ‘options’ for a reformed high street dental service, including core dental service models where existing funding is prioritised for essential care, according to the British Dental Association (BDA)

Health minister Robbie Butler said there was no prospect of further funding to save health service dentistry in Northern Ireland.

The BDA called for clarity about the future of the service for the sake of both the public and the profession.

‘Beyond breaking point’

Ciara Gallagher, chair of the BDA’s Northern Ireland Dental Practice Committee (NIDPC), said: ‘This service is beyond breaking point, and we are not being offered a lifeline.

‘Practitioners have been left with no choice but to make critical business decisions required to keep their practices afloat. The impact will be felt by those most in need of health service dentistry.

‘The absence of immediate support will have profound implications. We will of course not give up this fight, but it is abundantly clear that without sustainable funding, health service dentistry as we know it won’t have a future.’

Recent estimates suggest delivering Northern Irish health service dental care costs around £145 per hour while current funding only stretches to £90 – a shortfall of 60%.

In June, total patient registration in Northern Ireland dropped to an all-time low of 49%. In contrast, figures recorded at the same time in Scotland estimate that 95.1% of its population is registered with an NHS dentist.

New funding promised

This comes as funding has been announced for six additional dental foundation training places across Northern Ireland and a new emergency dental clinic in Omagh.

Supported by £787,000 of funding, the additional dental foundation training places bring the number available in Northern Ireland from 30 to 36 for 2026/7.

Chief dental officer for Northern Ireland Caroline Lappin said: ‘Investing in dental training is essential to building a strong and sustainable workforce. These additional places will provide newly qualified dentists with valuable clinical experience and encourage them to remain in health service practice.’

However, the BDA stresses that ‘these measures will do nothing to close the funding gap and will not improve access to routine dental care across Northern Ireland’.
